Research verified 2025-2026 Handbook flow. 0 — Introduction: What Gentoo Is (And Is Not) Welcome, new friend. If you know nothing about Gentoo , start here. Gentoo is a source-based Linux distribution. Most distributions give you prebuilt binaries. Gentoo gives you recipes called ebuilds and a package manager called Portage with its famous command emerge . You compile software for your machine with your flags. Result: total control, total learning, total responsibility. This means install takes hours, sometimes days. Tip: this is normal. Gentoo is a teacher that charges tuition in compile time. You will choose init system ( OpenRC default classic, or systemd ), USE flags (global options like -gnome -kde pulseaudio ), profile , kernel type, bootloader, filesystem. Nothing hidden. Who should install Gentoo ? Curious people who want to understand Linux from disk label to desktop pixel. Who should not? Anyone needing a 20 -minute install before a meeting. Tip: keep a second computer or phone nearby for docs and coffee. Official sources you will use constantly: Handbook:AMD64 overview, Full Installation guide, Gentoo Wiki , forums.gentoo.org , packages.gentoo.org , bugs.gentoo.org . Bookmark them now. Tip: never follow random blog commands blindly; always cross-check the Handbook version for your arch. Versions in this guide: arch amd64 , UEFI + GPT assumed, OpenRC default with systemd notes. What you need: 64 -bit PC, 4 GB RAM minimum ( 8 GB+ happy), 40 GB disk minimum ( 100 GB+ for desktop + sources), wired net preferred, 8 GB USB stick, backup of all data. Tip: wired Ethernet saves hours of Wi-Fi firmware pain on first install. Time: 1 evening for base, 1-2 days for desktop + kernel + hardening. Security mindset from zero: we will verify downloads, encrypt where sensible, harden kernel, use SELinux or AppArmor options, firewall with nftables , least privilege, updates. Tip: security is a process, not a package. Every step below has a security note. 1 — Boot Media, Networking, Disks Step 1 : get media from gentoo.org/downloads/amd64 . Two flavors: Minimal Installation CD (small, text only) and LiveGUI (graphical). Tip: newbies take LiveGUI for comfort, Minimal for focus. Both boot same Handbook path. Verify checksum/signature per Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Media . Write with balenaEtcher , Rufus , Ventoy , or dd . Example: dd if= install-amd64-minimal.iso of= /dev/sdX bs= 4M status=progress. Tip: triple-check /dev/sdX with lsblk or you wipe the wrong disk. Boot in UEFI mode if target is UEFI. Connect net: NetworkManager on LiveGUI, or net-setup / ip + wpa_supplicant on Minimal. Test with ping 8.8.8.8 and ping gentoo.org . Tip: if Wi-Fi needs firmware, plug cable now; fight Wi-Fi after install. Set sshd password if you want remote help, and set clock with chrony / ntpd . Step 2 — disks: see Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Disks . Use lsblk , fdisk -l , gdisk or parted . We assume UEFI + GPT. Layout: 1 GiB EFI System Partition FAT32, swap (match RAM if hibernate, else 4-8 GB ), rest for root ext4 or btrfs or xfs + optional /home . Tip: separate /home saves future reinstall pain. LUKS-encrypt root/home now if laptop — see Security chapter. Example with parted : mklabel gpt, mkpart ESP fat32 1MiB 1025MiB , set 1 esp on, mkpart swap 1025MiB 9GiB , mkpart root 9GiB 100% . Format: mkfs.fat -F32 /dev/nvme0n1p1 , mkswap + swapon , mkfs.ext4 or mkfs.btrfs -L gentoo . Mount root at /mnt/gentoo , mkdir /mnt/gentoo/efi and mount ESP there (Handbook UEFI path) or /boot for BIOS layout. Tip: mount ESP at /efi for systemd-boot/dist-kernel style, at /boot/efi only if you know why. Sources: Handbook Media, Handbook Disks, Arch Wiki EFI/GPT pages for background, Gentoo Wiki LUKS articles. Tip: photograph partition table with phone before formatting — future you says thanks. 2 — Stage3, Chroot, Portage Basics Step 3 — stage: a stage 3 is your seed system, separate from ISO. Pick at gentoo.org/downloads/amd64 matching init: stage3-amd64-openrc or stage3-amd64-systemd , multilib default, desktop flavor if graphical (name contains desktop). See Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Stage . Tip: desktop stage saves hours of USE-flag wrestling for GNOME/KDE. Download + .DIGESTS + .asc, verify with sha512sum and gpg . Unpack with tar xpvf stage3-*.tar.xz --xattrs-include='*.*' --numeric-owner inside /mnt/gentoo . Tip: --numeric-owner and xattrs are not optional; skipping breaks permissions. Step 4 — chroot: copy DNS: cp --dereference /etc/resolv.conf /mnt/gentoo/etc/ . Mount proc sys dev run or use arch-chroot /mnt/gentoo helper. For UEFI mount ESP at /efi before chroot. See Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Base . Inside: emerge-webrsync to fetch Portage tree snapshot, then optional emerge --sync . Read news with eselect news read . Tip: always read news before first big emerge; it warns about profile/migration breakage. Select profile: eselect profile list , eselect profile set N . Example desktop plasma or gnome , with systemd variant if needed. Check with eselect profile show . Configure make.conf : COMMON_FLAGS= -O2 -march=native -pipe , MAKEOPTS= -jN+1 where N =cores, USE flags, VIDEO_CARDS, INPUT_DEVICES, ACCEPT_LICENSE. Tip: -march=native is fast but binaries not portable; use generic x86-64 if you clone disks. Set eselect repository , mirrors with mirrorselect . Configure system files: /etc/fstab (use UUIDs from blkid ), hostname in /etc/conf.d/hostname ( OpenRC ) or /etc/hostname ( systemd ), timezone via eselect timezone / symlink /etc/localtime , locale in /etc/locale.gen + locale-gen + eselect locale , keymap, root password with passwd , networking ( NetworkManager easiest for desktop, dhcpcd / netifrc for servers). Tip: UUID in fstab prevents boot fail after disk reorder. Sources: Handbook Stage, Handbook Base, Wiki: Portage/Profiles , Wiki: MAKEOPTS , man make.conf , man emerge . Tip: keep a text log of every command; Gentoo forums love logs when helping. 3 — Kernel: Distribution vs Manual Compile See Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Kernel . Three roads: sys-kernel/gentoo-kernel-bin (prebuilt, fastest, great for newbies), sys-kernel/gentoo-kernel (source-built distro kernel, auto updates, needs installkernel + initramfs), sys-kernel/gentoo-sources (fully manual, you configure/compile). Tip: start with -bin to get to desktop today, switch to manual later for learning. Distro kernel path: emerge --ask sys-kernel/gentoo-kernel-bin sys-kernel/installkernel sys-kernel/dracut sys-firmware/linux-firmware sof-firmware sys-firmware/intel-microcode amd-ucode . Dracut builds initramfs for LUKS/LVM/btrfs. Check /efi or /boot for vmlinuz-6.x + initramfs . Tip: install linux-firmware + microcode before first boot or Wi-Fi/GPU may vanish. Enable installkernel USE for grub or systemd-boot layout. Manual path: emerge --ask sys-kernel/gentoo-sources sys-apps/pciutils usbutils , cd /usr/src/linux , make menuconfig (needs ncurses ). Essentials: 64 -bit, EFI stub, NVMe, SATA AHCI, ext4/btrfs built-in not module if root, drm amdgpu/i915/nouveau , sound, USB, networking. Tip: run lspci -k and lsmod on LiveGUI, photo it, enable exactly that hardware first. Build: make -j$(nproc) , make modules_install install . Takes 20 min to 2 hours by CPU. Keep .config backup in /root/kernel-config-YYYY-MM-DD . Initramfs when needed (LUKS/LVM/btrfs/UEFI): dracut --hostonly --kver 6.x.y-gentoo or genkernel --install initramfs . Verify ls -lh /boot /efi . Tip: if root is LUKS, test cryptsetup open before reboot or you lock yourself out. Sources: Handbook Kernel, Wiki: Kernel/Gentoo Kernel Upgrade Guide , Wiki: Dracut , Wiki: Genkernel , kernel.org docs. Tip: keep one known-good kernel + one new; never delete all old kernels. 4 — Bootloader, First Reboot, Post-Install Base See Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Bootloader . Default sys-boot/grub handles BIOS+UEFI. UEFI alt sys-boot/systemd-boot (simple, fast). Install: emerge --ask sys-boot/grub efibootmgr os-prober (skip os-prober if single boot). grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/efi --bootloader-id=Gentoo , then grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg . Tip: --efi-directory must match where you mounted ESP (/efi vs /boot); mismatch = unbootable. For systemd-boot : bootctl install --esp-path=/efi , loader entries in /efi/loader/entries/gentoo.conf pointing to vmlinuz + initramfs + root UUID + rw . Tip: systemd-boot needs manual entry update per kernel unless installkernel hooks do it — check after each upgrade. Exit chroot, unmount: exit , umount -l /mnt/gentoo/dev{/shm,/pts,} , umount -R /mnt/gentoo , reboot , remove USB. First boot: login root, check dmesg | grep -i -E 'error|firmware|fail' , ip a , ping . Add user: useradd -m -G wheel,audio,video,usb,portage -s /bin/bash alice , passwd alice , install sudo + visudo (uncomment wheel). Tip: never daily-drive as root; sudo + wheel from day one. Base update discipline: emerge --sync (or emaint sync -a ), emerge --ask --verbose --update --deep --newuse @world , emerge --depclean , revdep-rebuild , eclean-dist --deep . Tip: update weekly, read elog with eselect news + elogv; small frequent merges beat yearly breakage. Sources: Handbook Bootloader, Wiki: GRUB2 , Wiki: Systemd-boot , man sudoers . Tip: snapshot btrfs subvolume or Clonezilla image right after first good boot. 5 — Kernel Hardening, MAC, Toolchain Security Hardening is where Gentoo shines. Baseline: updated kernel ( 6.x stable, never ancient), least modules, Secure Boot with custom keys via sbctl or sbsigntools if threat model needs. Tip: enable Secure Boot only after normal boot works; debug one layer at a time. Kernel self-protection (manual or via gentoo-kernel + sysctl): enable STACKPROTECTOR_STRONG , STRICT_KERNEL_RWX , STRICT_MODULE_RWX , SLAB_FREELIST_HARDENED , SHUFFLE_PAGE_ALLOCATOR , RANDOMIZE_BASE (KASLR), HARDENED_USERCOPY , SECURITY_LOCKDOWN_LSM , PAGE_TABLE_ISOLATION , RETPOLINE / IBRS mitigations, DEBUG_WX to find WX, disable /dev/mem /dev/kmem , LDISC_AUTOLOAD off, USER_NS_UNPRIVILEGED restrict if not needing containers. Tip: copy hardened .config fragment to /root and diff after each make olddefconfig. See Wiki: Hardened Gentoo , gentoo-hardened overlay, KSPP checklists. Mandatory Access Control — pick one : SELinux (strongest, steepest; selinux-base-policy , relabel, setenforce 1 ) or AppArmor (easier, profiles via apparmor-utils , aa-enforce ) . Tip: newbies start with AppArmor + firewall; graduate to SELinux on second install. Add hardened malloc via sys-libs/mimalloc-hw or hardened_malloc overlay for browsers, firejail or bubblewrap sandbox for Firefox . Toolchain: gcc with -fstack-protector-strong -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -Wl,-z,RelRO,-z,Now -fPIE -pie via CFLAGS / LDFLAGS or hardened profile ( eselect profile hardened). Enable PIE + RELRO + NOW + SSP , verify with hardening-check / checksec . Tip: hardened flags can break exotic packages; keep per-package exceptions in /etc/portage/env, not global weaken. Boot/filesystem: LUKS2 ( cryptsetup ) with argon2id , detached header backup offline, fscrypt or eCryptfs only if needed, auditd rules for /etc/passwd /etc/shadow /boot , AIDE or samhain integrity DB on read-only USB. Tip: print LUKS recovery key on paper, store offsite; digital-only backup dies with disk. Sources: Gentoo Hardened project, Wiki: SELinux , Wiki: AppArmor , KSPP (kernel self-protection), man cryptsetup . Tip: change one hardening knob per reboot so you know what broke boot. 6 — Desktop: Plasma / GNOME, Graphics, Sound Pick profile first: eselect profile list | grep desktop , set default/linux/amd64/23.0/desktop/plasma or .../desktop/gnome (+ systemd variant if on systemd ). Set VIDEO_CARDS= amdgpu radeon intel nvidia as needed, INPUT_DEVICES= libinput synaptics . Tip: wrong VIDEO_CARDS = black screen; lspci | grep -i vga first. X or Wayland: xorg-server + xinit for classic, or Wayland via plasma-meta / gnome sessions. Install: emerge --ask kde-plasma/plasma-meta kde-apps/kdecore-meta sddm for KDE Plasma , or emerge --ask gnome-base/gnome gdm for GNOME . Lighter: i3 , sway , Xfce via xfce4-meta . Enable DM: rc-update add sddm default ( OpenRC ) or systemctl enable sddm ( systemd ). Tip: test with startx as user before enabling DM; DM hides errors. Firmware + microcode + graphics: linux-firmware amdgpu-ucode intel-microcode amd-ucode mesa vulkan-loader libva-vdpau-driver , kernel DRM built-in. Sound: pipewire wireplumber pipewire-pulse alsa-utils pavucontrol . Tip: PipeWire + WirePlumber is modern default; enable pipewire service per user. Fonts: noto , corefonts , fontconfig . Printing: cups . Bluetooth: bluez . Apps baseline: firefox (set USE=hardened pie ), thunderbird , libreoffice , vlc , gimp , keepassxc , flatpak optional for closed apps. Tip: Flatpak for Spotify/Discord/Steam keeps base clean; native emerge for everything else. Sources: Wiki: KDE , Wiki: GNOME , Wiki: Xorg , Wiki: PipeWire , eselect profile docs. Tip: emerge -pv before big desktop merge to see USE changes; veto surprises early. 7 — Network, Firewall, SSH, Updates, Backups Firewall default-deny with nftables (modern) or iptables legacy. Install nftables , enable, rules: allow lo , established, 22 only from LAN if needed, 80/443 out, drop rest, rate-limit SSH 3/min . Or use ufw / firewalld wrapper. Tip: test firewall over console first; lockout over SSH with no IPMI is a long walk. Add fail2ban for SSH, usbguard for BadUSB. SSH: openssh , PermitRootLogin no , PasswordAuthentication no (keys in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys 600 ), Port 2222 optional, AllowUsers alice . Tip: ssh-copy-id then disable passwords; one key leak beats thousand brute forces. VPN: wireguard-tools for road warriors. DNS: systemd-resolved or dnscrypt-proxy + DNSSEC. Updates + integrity: weekly emaint sync -a; emerge -uDN @world; emerge --depclean; revdep-rebuild; eclean-dist -d; updatedb; aide --check . Enable elogv / eselect news . Backups: borgbackup or restic to external LUKS disk + offsite, test restore quarterly. Tip: untested backup is rumor. Restore one file now to prove it works. Browser + user hardening: Firefox with uBlock Origin , NoScript or uMatrix , KeepassXC , separate profiles, bubblewrap / flatpak sandbox. Tip: Wayland + PipeWire + Flatpak Firefox is safest easy desktop sandbox. Sources: Wiki: Nftables , Wiki: OpenSSH , Wiki: WireGuard , Gentoo Security Handbook . Tip: run lynis audit or tiger check quarterly; fix reds first. 8 — Extra Security, Tips, Troubleshooting, Next Steps Extra: securelevel via sysctl kernel.kexec_load_disabled=1 kernel.dmesg_restrict=1 kernel.kptr_restrict=2 kernel.perf_event_paranoid=2 kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled=2 net.core.bpf_jit_harden=2 vm.mmap_rnd_bits=32 in /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf . sys-kernel/linux-firmware minimal (strip unused). Disable Bluetooth / Thunderbolt in BIOS if unused. Tip: sysctl + reboot + sysctl -a | grep setting to confirm; typos silently fail. Physical: BIOS password, boot order lock, LUKS + TPM2 + PIN via clevis optional, screen lock 5 min, usbguard block new devices when locked. Tip: encrypt swap or disable hibernate; cleartext swap leaks keys. Supply chain: verify ISOs, use gpg , app-portage/gemato , avoid random overlays; add eselect repository overlays sparingly. Troubleshooting: no boot? Check ESP mount, grub.cfg UUIDs, dracut --regenerate-all . Black screen? VIDEO_CARDS + firmware + eselect opengl . No net? dhcpcd vs NetworkManager conflict — pick one . Merge fail? Read build.log, emerge --info , search bugs.gentoo.org + forums with exact error. Tip: pastebin emerge --info + build log when asking help; helpers ignore vague 'it broke'. Next: join forums , IRC #gentoo , Reddit r/Gentoo , read GWN weekly news. Try distcc / ccache for speed, binpkg host for laptops. Tip: ccache size 10-20 GB cuts recompiles massively on desktop. Master source list: Handbook AMD64 + Full, Installation Media/Disks/Stage/Base/Kernel/Bootloader, Portage Profiles, KDE/GNOME/PipeWire/Nftables/OpenSSH/WireGuard/SELinux/AppArmor/Hardened Wiki pages, man pages for emerge make.conf fstab cryptsetup gpg sudoers sysctl . Tip: keep this HTML offline on USB; best rescue disk is docs you own. Gentoo installed? Harden weekly: emaint , emerge , eclean , aide , borgbackup . Tip: you now own your system — keep notes, keep backups, keep curiosity. Good luck from 0 to root.

japanDossier: Home Dossier · islands, eras, forms Dossier · the archipelago Japan: A Dossier on an Archipelago An island country of 124 million people, four-fifths of it mountains, sitting on four tectonic plates, that has twice rebuilt itself from fire — once in 1868 and once in 1945 — and that has produced one of the most distinctive material cultures on earth. This dossier follows the same four threads as its companion on China: the state, the language, the image and the household, from the Jōmon potters to the empty villages of 2026. Long read · 18 sections · sources at the end The archipelago Japan is not four islands and not one country in the way a continental state is. The recount of 2023 put the number of islands in Japanese territory at 14,125, of which about 430 are inhabited; four of them — Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, Shikoku — hold 97 per cent of the population. The total land area is 377,975 square kilometres, smaller than California, and about 73 per cent of it is mountain forest. The habitable plains are narrow, the rivers short and steep, and the sea between the islands is a highway rather than a barrier: the Inland Sea was the country's first commercial artery. The geology is the reason for almost everything else. The archipelago sits where the Pacific, Philippine, Eurasian and North American plates meet, which produces about 1,500 earthquakes a year that are felt, around 2,000 active faults, 111 active volcanoes and the hot springs that made bathing a national institution. Mount Fuji, at 3,776 metres, is a stratovolcano last active in 1707. The same subduction that builds the mountains also builds the tsunamis: the Tōhoku earthquake of 11 March 2011, magnitude 9.0, shifted Honshu two metres east and sent a wave into the coast that killed more than 18,000 people and destroyed the Fukushima Daiichi plant. That instability shaped the culture in ways that are easy to sentimentalise and hard to overstate. Buildings were traditionally light and replaceable, not monumental; the great shrine at Ise is rebuilt every twenty years from new timber on an adjacent plot, which is both a ritual of renewal and a practical response to rot and fire. Cities have burned repeatedly — Edo burned in 1657 and took 100,000 lives; Tokyo and Yokohama burned again in 1923 and in 1945 — and each time the rebuilding was faster and less ornamental than what it replaced. The political geography is now 47 prefectures, and the demographic one is a single corridor: the Tokaido belt from Tokyo through Nagoya to Osaka and Kobe holds more than half the population, with Tokyo's metropolitan area at about 37 million, the largest on earth. Outside that corridor, the country is emptying. There are around 8.5 million empty houses, akiya , and villages where the school, the post office and the bus have all closed. Japan , in the official view, is one nation with one language and one culture; the reality is a metropole and a periphery that no longer need each other. Jōmon, Yayoi, Kofun The Jōmon period (roughly 14,000 BCE to 300 BCE) is named for the cord marks pressed into its pottery, and that pottery is among the oldest in the world. These were hunter-gatherers, but not nomadic ones: they lived in pit houses, fished, gathered acorns and chestnuts, hunted deer and boar, and produced figurines — dogū , mostly female, some with goggles and swollen bellies — whose purpose no one knows. The famous flame-style vessels of the Middle Jōmon are the most exuberant ceramics any Neolithic culture made. Yayoi (300 BCE to 250 CE) brought wet-rice agriculture, bronze and iron, and a population that arrived in waves from the Korean peninsula, mixing with the Jōmon descendants. Rice changed everything: paddies need cooperation, irrigation needs organisation, and stored grain needs defending, which is the standard recipe for ranked societies. By the first century CE Chinese histories describe a country of a hundred kingdoms, and the Records of Wei describe one of them, Yamatai, ruled by a shamaness named Himiko, who sent envoys to the Chinese court and was buried with a hundred servants. The Kofun period (250–538) is named for the burial mounds: keyhole-shaped tumuli, some of them enormous — the tomb attributed to Emperor Nintoku near Osaka covers 32 hectares and is longer than the Great Pyramid is tall. The largest are imperial and cannot be excavated by law, which is convenient for a monarchy that prefers its origins mythological. By the end of the period the Yamato court, based in the Nara basin, had established itself as the dominant power, had a genealogy — the Kojiki of 712 and the Nihon Shoki of 720 — that traced the imperial line to the sun goddess, and had begun to import Chinese writing, Chinese administration and Chinese religion. What is worth noticing here is that Japan's foundational myths are written down in the eighth century, in a script borrowed from a country whose culture was already a thousand years older. The archipelago had a rich oral tradition and no writing of its own. Its literature begins as a translation project. The Chinese century Buddhism arrived officially in 538 or 552, depending on which chronicle you follow, as a gift from the king of Paekche in Korea; by the end of the century it was the religion of the court and the engine of state building. Prince Shōtoku (574–622), regent and legend, is credited with the Seventeen-Article Constitution of 604 — a set of injunctions to officials, in which "harmony" is the first virtue — and with the adoption of the Chinese calendar, the Chinese rank system and the Chinese model of a capital. The Taika reforms of 645 went further: land nationalised, taxes on rice, a census, a conscript army. The project was to make Japan a Chinese-style bureaucratic empire with a Japanese ruling house at the top. It did not last in that form. The Nara period (710–784) built a permanent capital, a grid city modelled on Chang'an, with the great temple of Tōdaiji and its bronze Buddha dedicated in 752, and it produced the Kojiki , the Nihon Shoki and the Man'yōshū , the first great anthology of Japanese poetry, in a script in which Chinese characters were used for their sound. Then the court moved to Heian-kyō — Kyoto — in 794 and, over the next four centuries, deliberately stopped looking at China. The Heian period (794–1185) is the most refined court culture in Japanese history, and the least like the rest of the country. The Fujiwara family governed as regents, marrying daughters into the imperial line; the emperor often abdicated young to rule as a cloistered monk; the provinces were left to their own gentry. At court, the arts were calligraphy, incense, poetry and taste. Two inventions made it possible: the simplification of Chinese characters into kana , a syllabary that could write Japanese as it was spoken, and the habit of writing in it. The result includes the Tale of Genji , written by Murasaki Shikibu around 1010, often called the first novel — a long, ironic, psychological narrative about court love with no plot in the modern sense; and Sei Shōnagon's Pillow Book , a collection of lists and observations that is the ancestor of the blog. Buddhism in this period went esoteric. Saichō and Kūkai travelled to Tang China in 804 and returned with Tendai and Shingon, two systems of ritual, mantra and mandala in which enlightenment could be reached through the body and the hand; Shingon's headquarters at Mount Kōya is still a cemetery town in the forest. The older Nara schools kept their scholarship, and the court kept both. The pattern — several Buddhist systems coexisting, each serving a different social function — never disappeared. The warrior centuries The Heian court lost control of the countryside in the twelfth century to the provincial warrior houses it had armed, and in 1185 Minamoto no Yoritomo defeated the Taira in the sea battle of Dan-no-ura and took power. In 1192 he was named shogun. The emperor remained in Kyoto as the source of legitimacy; the shogun governed from Kamakura, and the arrangement — a military government that derives its authority from a sacred but powerless court — lasted, with interruptions, until 1868. The Kamakura shogunate (1185–1333) was a government of warriors and their retainers, codified in the Jōei Code of 1232, a set of rules about land, inheritance and justice that is one of the earliest warrior law codes. It survived the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 — the second fleet was destroyed by a typhoon the Japanese called kamikaze , a divine wind — but the cost of the defence bankrupted the loyalty system, and in 1333 the shogunate fell. The Ashikaga shoguns who followed ruled from the Muromachi district of Kyoto through a century of civil war that culminated in the Ōnin War (1467–77), which destroyed most of the capital and opened 150 years of Sengoku , the "country at war", in which dozens of daimyō fought each other and the emperor sold calligraphy to survive. Out of that disorder came two of the country's most durable aesthetic forms, both products of Zen. The first is the Gozan system: the five great Zen monasteries ranked by the shogunate, which became the intellectual bureaucracy of the age and the channel through which Chinese painting, poetry and printing continued to arrive. The second is the aesthetic of restraint that runs from the tea room through the garden and the print: wabi , the beauty of the worn and the plain; sabi , the beauty of age; mono no aware , the pathos of things passing. Sen no Rikyū (1522–1591) formalised the tea ceremony as an exercise in humility — a small room, a rough bowl, a single flower — and was ordered to commit suicide by his patron Hideyoshi, which is the culture's own lesson about the relation between art and power. Unification came from three men in succession. Oda Nobunaga (1534–1582) broke the military power of the monasteries and the autonomous leagues; Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537–1598) completed the conquest, disarmed the peasantry in the "sword hunt" of 1588, and invaded Korea twice; Tokugawa Ieyasu won the battle of Sekigahara in 1600 and founded the shogunate that would rule for 265 years. The Tokugawa peace The Tokugawa order was a machine for preventing war, and it worked. The daimyō were ranked by their relation to the ruling house, forced to spend alternate years in Edo under the sankin kōtai system, and bound by marriage and hostage rules; their wives and heirs lived permanently in the shogun's capital. Roads, post stations and a uniform currency made the country a single market. The frontiers were closed to most foreign trade from the 1630s — the sakoku policy — with exceptions for the Dutch at Dejima in Nagasaki, the Chinese, and Korea through Tsushima. Christianity, which had arrived with Francis Xavier in 1549 and grown to perhaps 300,000 adherents, was suppressed with extraordinary violence at Shimabara in 1637–38 and then driven underground, where a hidden church survived for two centuries. Peace produced cities and a commercial culture. Edo grew to a million people by 1700, larger than London, and Osaka became the country's rice market, where futures contracts were traded from the 1730s. A merchant class with money and no political status spent it on pleasure: the licensed quarters, the theatre, the print. Ukiyo-e , "pictures of the floating world", began as advertisements for actors and courtesans and became, in the nineteenth century, one of the great achievements of world printmaking. Hokusai (1760–1849) made the Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji , including the wave; Hiroshige (1797–1858) made the road to Kyoto into a series that Van Gogh copied; Utamaro (1753–1806) made portraits of women that are also studies of the line. Literature found its own forms. Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694) took the seventeen-syllable haiku from a party game to a compressed meditation on time and travel, above all in Narrow Road to the Deep North . Ihara Saikaku wrote realistic novels of merchants and desire in the 1680s. Chikamatsu Monzaemon (1653–1725) wrote puppet plays about double suicides that are the Japanese equivalent of the Elizabethan stage. Literacy was high for a pre-industrial society — perhaps 30 to 40 per cent of men in the late period, more in cities — taught in thousands of temple schools. And the country was being studied from inside. Rangaku , "Dutch learning", made Western anatomy, astronomy and medicine available to a small circle of scholars in Nagasaki; the first Japanese dissection, in 1771, was recorded in a book that circulated widely. When the American squadron under Commodore Perry arrived in 1853 and demanded that the country open, the intellectual groundwork for what followed had already been laid — and so had the knowledge that the gap was real. Meiji, empire, defeat The Meiji Restoration of 1868 was not a revolution from below; it was a coup by a coalition of southwestern domains that replaced the shogunate with direct imperial rule and then used the emperor's restored authority to do what the shogunate had refused. The Charter Oath promised deliberative assemblies and the abandonment of "evil customs of the past". The Iwakura Mission of 1871–73 took half the government around the United States and Europe for eighteen months to study constitutions, factories and schools. Conscription was introduced in 1873, a national school system in 1872, the Meiji Constitution in 1889, and a parliament in 1890. The result was the fastest industrialisation of the nineteenth century. Textile mills, then shipyards, then railways; a state that built the infrastructure and then sold it to friendly businessmen, creating the zaibatsu ; a land tax that squeezed the peasantry to pay for it. Japan defeated China in 1894–95, took Taiwan, defeated Russia in 1904–05 — the first defeat of a European power by an Asian one in the modern era — annexed Korea in 1910, and entered the First World War on the Allied side to take German concessions in China. The 1920s were the country's democratic decade: party cabinets, universal male suffrage in 1925, a vibrant mass culture of cinema, radio, department stores and cafés. It ended with the Great Kantō earthquake of 1923, which killed about 105,000 people and was followed by massacres of Koreans by vigilantes, and with the collapse of export markets in 1929. The army, which answered to the emperor and not to the cabinet, took Manchuria in 1931 and turned it into a puppet state; junior officers assassinated politicians in 1932 and 1936; and from 1937 the country was at war with China in a conflict it could not end. Pearl Harbor in December 1941 opened the Pacific war. By 1945, sixty-six cities had been firebombed, Tokyo's March raid killed around 100,000 people in a night, and the atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August. The emperor announced surrender on 15 August. The reckoning with that period is incomplete and politically live: the Nanjing massacre, the comfort women system, forced labour, Unit 731 and the Yasukuni shrine, where convicted war criminals are among the enshrined. Official apologies have been issued and contested; textbook language is negotiated; the neighbours remember. A dossier that treats Japanese culture as pure aesthetics has skipped the century that produced the aesthetics' darkest patron. The postwar settlement The American occupation (1945–52) did five things that shaped the rest of the century. It dismantled the military and the colonial empire. It imposed a new constitution, drafted in a week by American lawyers and adopted in 1947, which made the emperor a symbol without political power, gave women the vote, and wrote Article 9: the renunciation of war as a sovereign right and of "land, sea, and air forces, as well as other war potential". It broke up the zaibatsu — partly, and then reversed course when the Cold War made Japan a forward base. It redistributed land to tenants, creating a conservative rural electorate that would keep the Liberal Democratic Party in power for most of the next seventy years. And it rebuilt the economy around a fixed exchange rate of 360 yen to the dollar, which made exports cheap. The growth that followed was the largest sustained expansion in modern history: from 1955 to 1973 the economy grew at close to 10 per cent a year. The mechanisms are worth naming because they became a global template. The Ministry of International Trade and Industry coordinated credit, licences and targets. The keiretsu — bank-centred corporate groups — spread risk across suppliers. Lifetime employment for regular workers, seniority pay and enterprise unions bought loyalty. Quality control, taught by an American statistician named W. Edwards Deming, became the Toyota Production System: just-in-time inventory, kaizen , andon cords that any worker could pull to stop the line. \n The high-water marks are visible: the Shinkansen opened in 1964, the year of the Tokyo Olympics; the bullet train, the transistor radio, the Walkman and the compact car made "Made in Japan" mean precision rather than imitation. By 1989 the Nikkei average reached 38,915 and Japanese banks held the largest deposits in the world; it was said that the grounds of the imperial palace were worth more than California. The long stagnation Then the bubble broke. The Bank of Japan raised rates in 1989–90, land prices fell, and the collateral behind the banking system evaporated. The Nikkei fell by more than 60 per cent over two years and did not regain its 1989 level for thirty-four years. What followed was not a depression but something less familiar: a slow, stubborn deflation, in which households postponed purchases because prices would be lower next year, firms repaid debt instead of investing, and the government ran deficits that kept the economy alive without restarting it. Economists call it a balance-sheet recession, and it became the reference case for the West after 2008. The social costs accumulated quietly. The lifetime employment system survived for the core of large firms and was withdrawn from everyone else: around 37 per cent of workers are now non-regular — part-time, contract, dispatched — with lower pay and no security. The generation that entered the labour market in the 1990s is called the "employment ice age" cohort, and it never caught up. The birth rate fell to 1.20 children per woman in 2023, deaths exceeded births by more than 800,000 a year, and the population is projected to fall below 100 million by the 2050s. The 65-and-over share passed 29 per cent, the highest of any large economy. Within that frame there are things that work better than outsiders assume. Health care is universal with a co-payment and no gatekeeping, and life expectancy is among the highest in the world. Trains run to the second. Violent crime is exceptionally low. The 2011 disaster produced a civic response that was studied worldwide. And the country's cultural production — manga, anime, games, fashion, food — has a global reach that its economy no longer has. Politics has been stable to the point of inertia: the LDP has governed for all but four years since 1955, through factions, farm subsidies and a fragmented opposition, and the country has been slow to liberalise immigration (about 3.4 million foreign residents, roughly 2.7 per cent), slow to raise the retirement age, and slow to change the tax base. In 2015 the government reinterpreted Article 9 to allow collective self-defence, and in 2022 committed to raising defence spending to 2 per cent of GDP by 2027 — the largest shift in security policy since 1945, and one that is still contested. The country's problem is not that it cannot reform; it is that it reforms at the speed of consensus, and the demographic clock is faster. kernelDisks: Home Kernel / Storage Kconfig Kconfig · disks, partitions, LVM, FAT32, NTFS Kernel disks: bring the disk up before anything else The storage stack is the one place where "make it a module" is answered by a single question: does the kernel need it before it can load modules? This page walks the storage menu from the block layer down to the filesystems — disk drivers, MSDOS_PARTITION and EFI_PARTITION , device mapper and LVM, FAT32 for the ESP, and both NTFS drivers — so each letter is a decision with a reason. <*> vs <M> GPT / MBR device mapper + LVM vfat + ntfs3 01 The one rule that decides the letter Networking can wait until userspace runs. Storage cannot: the kernel has to read the disk to find /sbin/init , and it has to read it with code that is already in memory . Whatever sits between the disk and the root mount is therefore a candidate for =y , and everything else is a cheap module you can unload. Marker Type Meaning <*> tristate, y Inside the kernel image; available before any module is loaded <M> tristate, m A .ko file; loadable, unloadable, and absent if /lib/modules is wrong < > tristate, n Not compiled at all — the code does not exist on this machine [*] boolean On or off; there is no module form, so the choice is real and permanent {M} forced Selected by another option; you cannot make it =y unless the parent is =y The practical test Ask: is this needed to mount the root filesystem, or to mount a filesystem that a boot service mounts before userspace can rescue the machine? If yes and there is no initramfs on the box — an appliance, a vendor image, a kernel you boot directly with -append root=/dev/nvme0n1p2 — then build it in. If no, a module costs one modprobe and saves memory on every machine that never touches it. The initramfs changes the arithmetic, and that is why most distributions ship all of this as modules: the initramfs carries sd_mod , dm-crypt , lvm and ext4 , loads them, and only then switches root. Build in what the image would need if the initramfs were broken or absent — which is exactly the failure mode you will meet at 3 a.m. 02 Where the truth lives Symbol names move between releases and the menu grouping is opinion, not documentation. The kernel tree defines every symbol; the running kernel can tell you what it was built with. # what this kernel says about itself uname -r zcat /proc/config.gz | grep -E "CONFIG_(EFI_PARTITION|BLK_DEV_DM|DM_CRYPT|VFAT_FS|NTFS3_FS)=" ls /boot/config-"$(uname -r)" 2>/dev/null # the authoritative definitions grep -n "config EFI_PARTITION" -A 10 block/partitions/Kconfig grep -rn "config NTFS3_FS" -A 14 fs/ntfs3/Kconfig grep -n "config FAT_DEFAULT_IOCHARSET" -A 8 fs/fat/Kconfig # change without menuconfig, then see exactly what moved cp .config .config.old scripts/config --file .config --enable EFI_PARTITION scripts/config --file .config --module VFAT_FS scripts/config --file .config --enable DM_INIT make olddefconfig scripts/diffconfig .config.old .config scripts/config --state CONFIG_X prints the current value without changing it, which is the quickest way to audit a vendor config before you trust it. And /proc/filesystems lists what the running kernel can actually mount — a name missing there is not a mount option problem. 03 The chain to the root filesystem Read it bottom-up: the bus driver finds the disk, the block layer exposes it, the partition parser splits it, the mapper (if any) reassembles it, and the filesystem driver reads it. Any missing link produces a VFS: Cannot open root device and a rescue prompt, with no clue about which link broke. Link Symbol Why built-in without an initramfs Block layer BLOCK [*] Everything below is inside it; it is not optional Disk driver BLK_DEV_SD , BLK_DEV_NVME , VIRTIO_BLK The root disk is not visible at all until this loads Partition table EFI_PARTITION , MSDOS_PARTITION The disk appears, but no p1 / p2 nodes exist Mapper BLK_DEV_DM , DM_CRYPT , LVM targets Root on LUKS or on an LV is unreachable without it Filesystem EXT4_FS , XFS_FS , BTRFS_FS VFS: Cannot open root device even though it is there Two links that fail quietly A missing partition parser is worse than a missing driver, because the disk still shows up: you get /dev/nvme0n1 , no partitions, and a filesystem signature nobody can mount. A missing filesystem looks like "root device not found" too, even though lsblk is perfectly happy. Both are one grep away in /proc/config.gz . 04 Disk drivers: SD, NVMe, virtio # SCSI/ATA low level CONFIG_BLK_DEV_SD=y # sd_mod: the sdX names, ATA and USB UAS disk CONFIG_ATA=y CONFIG_SATA_AHCI=y CONFIG_ATA_PIIX=y # IDE-emulated mode in older QEMU CONFIG_SCSI=y CONFIG_SCSI_VIRTIO=y # virtio-scsi controller # NVMe CONFIG_BLK_DEV_NVME=y # the whole nvme stack; no sdX alias # virtual and removable CONFIG_VIRTIO_BLK=y CONFIG_MMC_BLOCK=m # SD cards and eMMC CONFIG_MMC_SDHCI=m CONFIG_USB_STORAGE=m CONFIG_BLK_DEV_SR=m # optical / srX, needed to read install media CONFIG_UAS=m # USB Attached SCSI, much faster than usb-storage Note that BLK_DEV_SD is not "the SATA driver": it is the SCSI disk class driver, and every SATA disk in AHCI mode, every USB mass-storage device and every virtio-scsi disk goes through it. A kernel with SATA_AHCI but without BLK_DEV_SD finds the controller and shows no disk at all — the most common "my build does not see the disk" answer. NVMe is different: BLK_DEV_NVME registers its own block device, so there is no dependency on sd_mod . On a machine that boots from NVMe with no initramfs, this one symbol must be =y , and it is worth building in even with an initramfs, because the initramfs is written from the module list of the machine that generated it. 05 Partitions — and the one everybody forgets CONFIG_PARTITION_ADVANCED=y # [*] the gate for everything below CONFIG_EFI_PARTITION=y # GPT — modern disks, and the reason pN vanished CONFIG_MSDOS_PARTITION=y # MBR — USB sticks, old VMs, hybrid images CONFIG_OF_PARTITION=y # devicetree partitions, ARM boards CONFIG_BSD_DISKLABEL=m CONFIG_SOLARIS_X86_PARTITION=m CONFIG_UNIXWARE_DISKLABEL=m Symbol Form Symptom when missing EFI_PARTITION bool [*] GPT disk shows as one device; lsblk lists no children MSDOS_PARTITION bool [*] MBR USB stick mounts only as a whole disk PARTITION_ADVANCED bool [*] The exotic parsers are not even offered in the menu BLK_DEV_LOOP tristate mount -o loop image.iso fails; snap and AppImage break BLK_DEV_NBD tristate Network block devices unavailable BLK_DEV_RAM tristate No /dev/ram0 ; some rescue tooling assumes it These are booleans, so "make GPT a module" is not on the table: either the kernel understands GPT or it does not. Build both parsers in. MSDOS_PARTITION costs a few kilobytes and is the difference between a rescue stick that mounts and one that does not. Hybrid and 4K-sector disks A hybrid MBR/GPT image needs both parsers, and a 4Kn disk needs nothing extra in the config — but a partition table written for 512-byte sectors on a 4K-native disk will be rejected, and the message is about the partition table, not about Kconfig. Check with blockdev --getss /dev/sdX . 06 Block layer extras worth building Symbol Recommended What it buys BLK_DEV_INITRD =y Initramfs support; without it no modern distro kernel boots BLK_DEV_BSG =m sg3_utils , smartctl , SCSI generic access BLK_CGROUP =y I/O limits per container and per systemd slice IOSCHED_BFQ =m Desktop fairness; the scheduler itself is optional MQ_IOSCHED_KYBER =m Low-latency reads on NVMe BLK_DEV_THROTTLING =y Per-cgroup IOPS and bandwidth caps BLK_DEV_INTEGRITY =y if T10-PI End-to-end data integrity on enterprise disks BLK_DEV_WRITE_MOUNTED =n Refuses writes to a mounted block device — a real footgun closed BLK_DEV_WRITE_MOUNTED is recent and worth knowing: with it enabled (the historical default) root can still dd over a mounted filesystem and corrupt it. Disabling it turns a silent disaster into an EBUSY , which is the kind of change a kernel config makes better than any warning banner. 07 Device mapper and LVM The first correction: there is no CONFIG_LVM . LVM is a userspace tool ( lvm2 ) that drives the kernel's device-mapper targets; the kernel side is a handful of DM_* symbols. Searching a config for LVM and finding nothing is not a missing feature. CONFIG_MD=y CONFIG_BLK_DEV_DM=y # =y if root is on LVM/LUKS and there is no initramfs CONFIG_DM_INIT=y # [*] activate DM devices at boot, before the root mount CONFIG_DM_CRYPT=y # LUKS CONFIG_DM_SNAPSHOT=m # thin snapshots, backup windows CONFIG_DM_THIN_PROVISIONING=m # the modern LVM thin pool CONFIG_DM_CACHE=m # SSD cache in front of a slow LV CONFIG_DM_MIRROR=m CONFIG_DM_RAID=m CONFIG_DM_VERITY=m # read-only verified root images CONFIG_DM_INTEGRITY=m CONFIG_DM_MULTIPATH=m # two paths to the same SAN LUN CONFIG_DM_ZERO=m # sparse test devices # md/RAID is a different subsystem, do not confuse it with DM RAID CONFIG_MD_RAID0=m CONFIG_MD_RAID1=m CONFIG_MD_RAID456=m Symbol Form Missing it means BLK_DEV_DM tristate dmsetup cannot open /dev/mapper/control ; no LVM at all DM_INIT bool [*] Root on an LV needs an initramfs; without one, boot hangs at the root prompt DM_CRYPT tristate crypt: unknown target type ; LUKS unlock impossible DM_THIN_PROVISIONING tristate lvcreate --thin fails; the thin pool target is unknown DM_CACHE , DM_RAID tristate Only that LV type refuses to activate; the rest of LVM works MD_RAID456 tristate mdadm assembles nothing for RAID5/6 Build BLK_DEV_DM , DM_CRYPT and the thin target in when the root volume lives on them and the machine has no initramfs. Otherwise they are modules and the initramfs loads them — that is what update-initramfs is for, and why a kernel upgrade with a broken initramfs is a separate failure from a bad config. 08 LUKS and the crypto that must exist first DM_CRYPT=y is only half of an encrypted root. The cipher the volume was created with must be available at unlock time, and the defaults are not free: aes-xts-plain64 needs AES and XTS, and the key derivation needs a hash. CONFIG_DM_CRYPT=y CONFIG_CRYPTO_AES=y CONFIG_CRYPTO_XTS=y CONFIG_CRYPTO_SHA256=y CONFIG_CRYPTO_USER_API_SKCIPHER=m # only if userspace asks for ciphers by name CONFIG_KEYS=y CONFIG_ENCRYPTED_KEYS=y # systemd asks for a TPM-bound key CONFIG_BLK_INLINE_ENCRYPTION=m # eMMC/UFS hardware encryption The failure that looks like a wrong password cryptsetup: device-mapper: reload ioctl on … failed: Invalid argument during unlock is usually not a password problem: it is the cipher or hash module missing from the initramfs. Check /proc/crypto for xts(aes) before deciding the disk is lost. File-level encryption is a different stack: FS_ENCRYPTION (fscrypt) encrypts directories inside ext4 and F2FS and needs no device mapper at all, while DM_VERITY gives a read-only root whose blocks are hash-verified — the usual basis of an immutable appliance image. 09 FAT32: the format that boots machines FAT is not a legacy detail you can drop. The EFI system partition is FAT, most boot media is FAT, and camera cards, dashcams and firmware updaters are FAT. Three symbols do the work, and a fourth decides which characters survive the trip. CONFIG_FAT_FS=y # the core; vfat and msdos depend on it CONFIG_VFAT_FS=y # long names, the usual "vfat" — and the ESP CONFIG_MSDOS_FS=m # 8.3 names, FAT12/16; usually not needed CONFIG_EXFAT_FS=m # large cards, a different driver entirely # the charset housekeeping people skip CONFIG_NLS_CODEPAGE_437=y CONFIG_NLS_ISO8859_1=y CONFIG_NLS_UTF8=y CONFIG_FAT_DEFAULT_CODEPAGE=437 CONFIG_FAT_DEFAULT_IOCHARSET="utf8" Symbol Form Missing it means FAT_FS tristate unknown filesystem type 'vfat' ; fat is not even in /proc/filesystems VFAT_FS tristate The mount type named vfat does not exist — the common case MSDOS_FS tristate Only mount -t msdos fails; vfat still mounts the same disk NLS_UTF8 tristate, no prompt FAT-fs: IO charset utf8 not found , then unreadable names NLS_CODEPAGE_437 tristate Default codepage unavailable; the mount falls back or fails EXFAT_FS tristate Big SD cards need exfat / exfatprogs instead of vfat FAT_DEFAULT_IOCHARSET is a string, not a module, and it is the one setting that decides whether a Portuguese or Japanese filename appears intact. "utf8" is the right default for anything shared with another operating system; "iso8859-1" is the historic default and produces replacement characters on any name outside Latin-1. Is vfat boot-critical? Only on machines whose /boot is the ESP itself — some ARM boards, some unified-kernel images, and every setup that keeps kernels on the ESP. On ordinary x86 with a separate ext4 /boot , the firmware reads FAT and the kernel never does, so <M> is correct and expected. 10 NTFS: ntfs3 against the legacy driver Two kernel drivers carry the NTFS name and they are not the same thing. NTFS3_FS is the in-kernel read-write driver; NTFS_FS is the old read-mostly one that most people replaced years ago with the userspace FUSE driver ntfs-3g . Symbol What it is Recommended NTFS3_FS In-kernel driver, read-write, mount type ntfs3 <M> ; <*> only if mounted before modules load NTFS3_LZX_XPRESS Decompression for compressed NTFS files <M> when the volume uses compression NTFS_FS Legacy driver, mount type ntfs < > unless you have a reason NTFS_RW Limited write support for the legacy driver < > — it is the one that damages volumes NLS_UTF8 Charset for non-ASCII filenames <*> or <M> , same reasoning as FAT # the modern driver CONFIG_NTFS3_FS=m CONFIG_NTFS3_LZX_XPRESS=m # the legacy pair — leave both off # CONFIG_NTFS_FS is not set # CONFIG_NTFS_RW is not set # mount it, and check the driver that answered mount -t ntfs3 /dev/sdb1 /mnt/win findmnt -no FSTYPE,SOURCE /mnt/win What neither driver opens BitLocker volumes and disks in Intel RST / RAID mode are not NTFS volumes to the kernel: the encryption or the Intel metadata sits below the filesystem and no NTFS* symbol helps. Those need the volume unlocked in firmware first, which is a different page and a different failure. ntfs3 also handles the hibernated/fast-startup case badly: a Windows volume that was not shut down properly still looks dirty, and the driver will mount it read-only rather than risk a corrupted $LogFile . That is the intended behaviour, not a config problem — dmesg | grep ntfs3 says so in one line. 11 Filesystems you actually mount Symbol Recommended Where it appears EXT4_FS =y if root Almost every Debian and Ubuntu root; also /boot XFS_FS =m RHEL-family roots and large data volumes BTRFS_FS =m Snapshots, subvolumes, openSUSE/Fedora defaults F2FS_FS =m Flash-only devices, phones, some handhelds SQUASHFS =m Live images, snap packages, read-only overlays ISO9660_FS , UDF_FS =m CD/DVD and Blu-ray; UDF also covers large optical media TMPFS =y /dev/shm and /run ; systemd needs it early OVERLAY_FS =m Containers and live-system persistence FUSE_FS =m ntfs-3g, sshfs, rclone, and every userspace filesystem TMPFS is the odd one out in this table: it is not a disk filesystem, but a machine that cannot mount /run early does not reach a login prompt. Treat it like the console — always in. 12 Software that asks for the module A symbol name says nothing until you know which program calls it. The left column is the module, the middle is the software that fails without it, and the right is what that program is doing with it. If none of the software in a row is installed here, that module has no purpose on this machine. a VM snapshot needs the target present dm_snapshot lvm2 ( lvcreate -s ) Copy-on-write snapshots taken before an upgrade dm_multipath multipath-tools ( multipathd ) Two HBAs, one LUN; without it the second path becomes a second disk dm_verity veritysetup (cryptsetup package), systemd-veritysetup Hash-verified read-only images dm_integrity integritysetup Per-block checksums under a filesystem loop snapd , flatpak , AppImage, mount -o loop Mounts a file as if it were a disk; kernelNetworking: Home Kernel / Networking Kconfig Kconfig · built-in vs module, symbol by symbol Kernel networking: what goes in, what gets loaded Every networking failure that begins with "operation not supported" is usually a symbol set to the wrong letter years earlier. This page explains the three markers in make menuconfig , gives the rule that decides built-in versus module, and then walks the networking menu option by option — routing tables, netfilter, bridges, tunnels, traffic control and eBPF — so the choice is a reason, not a reflex. <*> vs <M> policy routing netfilter + nftables tc / XDP 01 The markers, and what (*) really is The notation is the first thing tutorials blur. There is no (*) symbol in the kernel config; menuconfig draws three different markers, and confusing them is how people "enable routing" by ticking a boolean that only controls whether a module is even offered. You see Symbol type Means Can be unloaded? <*> tristate, value y Compiled into the kernel image No <M> tristate, value m Compiled as a separate .ko Yes, unless in use < > tristate, value n Not built at all — [*] boolean On or off only; there is no module form No {M} / {*} forced Selected by another option you enabled Only by disabling the parent That table answers half the question by itself: many routing features are booleans , so they show as [*] and cannot be modules at all. Where a symbol is a tristate, the decision is real. The rule that decides everything Build in what the machine needs before it can load modules ; make everything else a module. In practice: storage, console, the NIC the initramfs brings up, and anything the initramfs needs to reach the root filesystem. Networking beyond that is almost always a module — unless you intend to burn the bridge by disabling module loading. 02 Where the truth lives Never trust a blog for a symbol name — including this one. The kernel tree names its own symbols, and the running kernel can tell you what it was built with. # what am I running, and was this config even exposed? uname -r zcat /proc/config.gz | grep -E "CONFIG_(IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES|NF_CONNTRACK)=" ls /boot/config-"$(uname -r)" # the authoritative definition, in the source tree grep -n "config IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES" -A 12 net/ipv4/Kconfig scripts/config --file .config --state CONFIG_BRIDGE # change the config without menuconfig scripts/config --file .config --module BRIDGE make olddefconfig # resolve new symbols with defaults scripts/diffconfig .config.old .config # exactly what you changed localmodconfig is tempting — it keeps only the modules currently loaded. It is fine for a laptop, and a trap for a router: the modules your firewall needs may simply not be loaded on the build machine when you run it. 03 What must be built in Symbol Why it cannot be a module here VIRTIO_NET Cloud and VM images whose root disk is virtual need the NIC before root mounts E1000E , IGB , IXGBE The physical port used for PXE, NFS root or iSCSI boot BRIDGE Only if the root filesystem is behind a bridge (rare) or modules are disabled VLAN_8021Q When the management interface is tagged and configured in the initramfs BONDING When the boot interface is a bond PACKET If the machine's only diagnostic is tcpdump on a rescue image with no modules Everything else on this page is a module in a sane configuration. The price of =y is permanent memory and a permanently larger trusted computing base; the price of =m is a load step and the risk that the module is not there after a kernel upgrade. 04 Routing and policy routing # Networking support -> Networking options CONFIG_NET=y # [*] the whole stack CONFIG_INET=y # [*] TCP/IP CONFIG_IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER=y # [*] unlocks the routing extras below CONFIG_IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y # [*] ip rule, policy routing CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH=y # [*] several nexthops per route CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_CLASSID=y # [*] tc classification by route CONFIG_IPV6_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y # [*] the same for IPv6 CONFIG_IPV6_SUBTREES=y # [*] source-based IPv6 lookups Symbol Form Turn it on when IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER bool [*] Always on a router or firewall; it gates the rest IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES bool [*] You use ip rule , VRFs, or anything with multiple routing tables IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH bool [*] Two uplinks, or the ECMP lab from the GNS3 page IP_ROUTE_CLASSID bool [*] Traffic control keyed on a route class IPV6 tristate You have IPv6 — build in if the address is assigned before modules load These are booleans, so "make it a module" is not an option and the question becomes whether to enable them at all. A kernel without IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES still routes; it just ignores every second table, and ip rule commands appear to succeed while doing nothing. 05 Netfilter, conntrack, NAT # core: everything else depends on these CONFIG_NETFILTER=y CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK=m <M> the state table CONFIG_NF_NAT=m <M> NAT engine, needed by MASQUERADE CONFIG_NF_TABLES=m <M> the nftables core CONFIG_NF_TABLES_INET=m <M> one table for v4 and v6 CONFIG_NFT_CT=m <M> ct expression CONFIG_NETFILTER_XTABLES=m <M> the xtables compatibility layer CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_MASQUERADE=m CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK_FTP=m # helpers: load only what you need Symbol Form Effect if missing NF_CONNTRACK tristate No stateful rules, no NAT, no conntrack tool NF_NAT tristate MASQUERADE and DNAT simply do not exist NF_TABLES tristate nft reports no such file or unsupported NETFILTER_XTABLES tristate Legacy iptables rules fail to apply NF_CONNTRACK_FTP etc. tristate Only that protocol's helper is absent — good default Modules are fine here — until you disable modules Debian and every mainstream distro ship netfilter as modules, and it works. Build it in when you plan to set kernel.modules_disabled=1 after boot, or when the firewall must be able to drop packets before any userspace process has run. 06 Bridges, VLANs, bonds, virtual links Symbol Recommended Needed by BRIDGE <M> Anything that bridges: VMs, containers, the GNS3 switch BRIDGE_NETFILTER <M> iptables on bridged traffic; Docker needs it VLAN_8021Q <M> ip link add ... type vlan BONDING <M> LACP and failover bonds MACVLAN / IPVLAN <M> Many addresses on one NIC, container networking VETH <M> Namespaces, containers, test topologies DUMMY <M> A stable interface that stays up with no cable IFB <M> Ingress shaping — redirecting ingress into a qdisc TUN <M> VPNs and user-space tunnels; also creates tap These are cheap modules and there is no security reason to build them in. The one exception is a host that cannot load modules at all, where every link type the boot scripts create must be present in the image. 07 Tunnels and VPNs Symbol Recommended Note WIREGUARD <M> One module, no dependencies; "Unknown device type" means it is missing VXLAN <M> Overlay networks; needs a UDP tunnel port GENEVE <M> The newer overlay encapsulation NET_IPIP <M> Simple IPv4-in-IPv4 NET_IPGRE <M> GRE, including the keyed form IPV6_SIT <M> IPv6 in IPv4, legacy but still used XFRM_USER , INET_ESP <M> IPsec; the user interface plus the ESP transform INET_AH <M> Authentication header, rarely the right choice today Tunnels are the classic "loads on demand" case: the interface type is requested by name from userspace, and the kernel autoloads the module. If autoloading is disabled, the module has to be in the image or loaded explicitly at boot. 08 Traffic control and eBPF CONFIG_NET_SCHED=y CONFIG_NET_SCH_HTB=m CONFIG_NET_SCH_CAKE=m CONFIG_NET_SCH_FQ_CODEL=m CONFIG_NET_SCH_INGRESS=m # the hook for clsact CONFIG_NET_CLS_ACT=y # [*] actions are not optional once you classify CONFIG_NET_ACT_MIRRED=m # redirect: ingress shaping, mirroring CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER=m # hardware-offloadable matching CONFIG_NET_CLS_U32=m CONFIG_NET_CLS_BPF=m CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL=y # [*] required by every eBPF tool CONFIG_BPF_JIT=y CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF=y # [*] libbpf CO-RE needs this NET_SCHED and BPF_SYSCALL are booleans; the qdiscs and classifiers are modules. A "qdisc not found" error is a missing sch_*.ko , while "Operation not supported" on a flower filter is a missing cls_flower.ko — two different messages, two different symbols. XDP is a driver property, not just a config option eBPF itself is in the core, but XDP offload needs driver support and, for the native path, a driver that implements it. On veth and tun you get the generic path; on a card that does not support it, the program simply will not attach natively. 09 Sockets that let you see Symbol Recommended Tool that breaks without it PACKET <M> tcpdump , Snort afpacket, Suricata INET_DIAG <M> ss , socket listings in monitoring agents INET_TCP_DIAG , INET_UDP_DIAG <M> Per-protocol detail for ss -t / -u UNIX_DIAG <M> ss -x NETLINK_DIAG <M> Netlink socket inspection IKCONFIG + IKCONFIG_PROC [*] /proc/config.gz — without it, no way to audit the build IKCONFIG is the cheapest hardening decision on this page: it embeds the config so anyone can check what was built, including you, two years later. Hide it if the config itself is sensitive; keep it if you would rather be auditable. 10 Options that harden by removing CONFIG_MODULE_SIG=y CONFIG_MODULE_SIG_FORCE=y # refuse unsigned modules entirely CONFIG_MODULE_UNLOAD=n # nothing can be unloaded CONFIG_KEXEC=n CONFIG_STRICT_KERNEL_RWX=y CONFIG_DEBUG_WX=y # runtime, after everything is loaded sysctl -w kernel.modules_disabled=1 MODULE_SIG_FORCE makes every module signed and trusted; a third-party driver you built yourself needs a key in the kernel keyring. MODULE_UNLOAD=n removes the ability to replace a loaded module — and the ability to recover from a bad one without rebooting. modules_disabled=1 is the strongest and least reversible: after it, no module loads. Everything the machine will ever need must already be loaded or built in. Do the arithmetic before the reboot A router that disables modules at boot must have bridging, VLAN, conntrack and the firewall built in — and the tests on this page run before the setting is permanent. The usual outcome of doing it in the other order is a machine that powers on and never passes a packet again. 11 Three role fragments These are starting points for make olddefconfig , not gospel: symbol names and defaults move between versions, and your hardware decides the driver lines. # A. Router / firewall (Debian, netfilter as modules) CONFIG_NET=y CONFIG_INET=y CONFIG_IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER=y CONFIG_IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH=y CONFIG_NETFILTER=y CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK=m CONFIG_NF_NAT=m CONFIG_NF_TABLES=m CONFIG_NETFILTER_XTABLES=m CONFIG_BRIDGE=m CONFIG_VLAN_8021Q=m # B. Virtualisation host (everything a guest might ask for) CONFIG_BRIDGE=m CONFIG_BRIDGE_NETFILTER=m CONFIG_VETH=m CONFIG_TUN=m CONFIG_MACVLAN=m CONFIG_VXLAN=m CONFIG_OPENVSWITCH=m # C. Hardened appliance (modules disabled after boot) CONFIG_VIRTIO_NET=y CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK=y CONFIG_NF_NAT=y CONFIG_NF_TABLES=y CONFIG_IP_NF_IPTABLES=y CONFIG_BRIDGE=y CONFIG_PACKET=y CONFIG_MODULE_SIG_FORCE=y CONFIG_IKCONFIG=y CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC=y The pattern is visible: same features, different letter. A is the mainstream choice and the easiest to maintain; C is the one you can reason about at the packet level, at the cost of never being able to add a feature without a rebuild. 12 Prove the build # what is actually in this kernel zcat /proc/config.gz | grep -E "IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES|NF_CONNTRACK|BRIDGE|PACKET" lsmod | grep -E "nf_|bridge|vlan" # each subsystem, asked the only way that counts ip rule add fwmark 1 table 100; ip rule show # policy routing nft list tables # nftables iptables -t nat -L -n | head -3 # legacy NAT table tc qdisc show dev lo # traffic control ip link add vtest type veth peer name vtest2 # veth tcpdump -i any -c1 -w /dev/null 2>&1 # AF_PACKET conntrack -L 2>/dev/null | wc -l # state table ss -s # socket diag Check Good sign What a failure tells you ip rule add Rule listed IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES off — the rule "works" but is ignored nft list tables Empty list, no error NF_TABLES missing iptables -t nat Table prints NF_NAT or xtables missing tcpdump One packet captured PACKET missing: every sensor on the box is blind ip link add veth Pair created VETH missing Run the same set after every kernel upgrade. The build you audited is not the build that boots tomorrow — check the external references for the current symbol names when the output disagrees with the page. 13 Failure table Symptom Missing symbol Fix tcpdump: socket: Address family not supported PACKET <M> and load af_packet iptables: Table does not exist NF_NAT / IP_NF_NAT Enable NAT, reload the firewall nft: no such file or directory NF_TABLES Build the nftables core, not just xtables A rule in table 100 is ignored IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES Boolean: rebuild required RTNETLINK answers: Operation not supported on a filter NET_CLS_FLOWER Load the classifier module Unknown device type for wg0 WIREGUARD Module, not a userspace package iptables rules never see bridged frames BRIDGE_NETFILTER Enable, then check br_netfilter is loaded Works until reboot after an upgrade Running kernel ≠ /lib/modules Reboot into the new image, or pin the kernel A module cannot be loaded at all MODULE_SIG_FORCE or modules_disabled Sign it, or rebuild everything in 14 Sources Kernel networking — the authoritative documentation for routing, netfilter and tc. Debian security Networking Snort Início Kernel / Kconfig de rede Kconfig · built-in ou módulo, símbolo a símbolo Rede no kernel: o que entra na imagem e o que é carregado Quase todas as falhas de rede que começam com «operation not supported» são um símbolo com a letra errada, escolhida anos antes. Esta página explica os três marcadores do make menuconfig , dá a regra que decide entre built-in e módulo e percorre o menu de rede opção a opção — tabelas de rotas, netfilter, bridges, túneis, controlo de tráfego e eBPF — para a escolha ser uma razão e não um reflexo. <*> vs <M> rotas por política netfilter + nftables tc / XDP 01 Os marcadores e o que é (*) A notação é a primeira coisa que os tutoriais baralham. Não existe um símbolo (*) na configuração do kernel: o menuconfig desenha três marcadores diferentes, e confundi-los é como alguém «ativa o encaminhamento» carregando num booleano que só controla se um módulo é sequer oferecido. Vê Tipo de símbolo Significa Pode descarregar? <*> tristate, valor y Compilado dentro da imagem do kernel Não <M> tristate, valor m Compilado como .ko separado Sim, se não estiver em uso < > tristate, valor n Não é compilado de todo — [*] booleano Só ligado ou desligado; não há forma de módulo Não {M} / {*} forçado Selecionado por outra opção que ativou Só desativando o pai Essa tabela responde a metade da pergunta: muitas funcionalidades de encaminhamento são booleanas , aparecem como [*] e não podem ser módulos. Onde o símbolo é tristate, a decisão é real. A regra que decide tudo Compile dentro o que a máquina precisa antes de conseguir carregar módulos ; o resto é módulo. Na prática: armazenamento, consola, a NIC que o initramfs levanta e tudo o que o initramfs precisa para chegar à raiz. Rede para além disso é quase sempre módulo — a menos que pretenda desativar o carregamento de módulos de vez. 02 Onde está a verdade Nunca confie num blog para um nome de símbolo — incluindo este. A árvore do kernel nomeia os seus símbolos, e o kernel em execução sabe com o que foi compilado. # o que estou a correr, e a configuração foi exposta? uname -r zcat /proc/config.gz | grep -E "CONFIG_(IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES|NF_CONNTRACK)=" ls /boot/config-"$(uname -r)" # a definição autoritária, na árvore de código grep -n "config IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES" -A 12 net/ipv4/Kconfig scripts/config --file .config --state CONFIG_BRIDGE # mudar a configuração sem menuconfig scripts/config --file .config --module BRIDGE make olddefconfig # resolver símbolos novos com omissões scripts/diffconfig .config.old .config # exatamente o que mudou localmodconfig é tentador — mantém só os módulos carregados. Serve para um portátil e é uma armadilha para um router: os módulos de que a firewall precisa podem simplesmente não estar carregados na máquina de compilação quando o corre. 03 O que tem de ser built-in Símbolo Porque não pode ser módulo aqui VIRTIO_NET Imagens de cloud e VM com disco virtual precisam da NIC antes da raiz montar E1000E , IGB , IXGBE A porta física usada para PXE, raiz NFS ou boot iSCSI BRIDGE Só se a raiz estiver atrás de uma bridge (raro) ou com módulos desativados VLAN_8021Q Quando a interface de gestão é etiquetada e configurada no initramfs BONDING Quando a interface de arranque é um bond PACKET Se o único diagnóstico da máquina é tcpdump numa imagem de resgate sem módulos Todo o resto desta página é módulo numa configuração sensata. O preço de =y é memória permanente e uma base de confiança maior; o preço de =m é um passo de carregamento e o risco de o módulo não existir depois de uma atualização do kernel. 04 Rotas e rotas por política # Networking support -> Networking options CONFIG_NET=y # [*] a pilha inteira CONFIG_INET=y # [*] TCP/IP CONFIG_IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER=y # [*] destranca o resto abaixo CONFIG_IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y # [*] ip rule, rotas por política CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH=y # [*] vários nexthops por rota CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_CLASSID=y # [*] classificação tc pela rota CONFIG_IPV6_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y # [*] o mesmo para IPv6 CONFIG_IPV6_SUBTREES=y # [*] procuras IPv6 por origem Símbolo Forma Ativar quando IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER bool [*] Sempre num router ou firewall; abre caminho ao resto IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES bool [*] Usa ip rule , VRFs ou várias tabelas IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH bool [*] Dois uplinks, ou o ECMP do laboratório GNS3 IP_ROUTE_CLASSID bool [*] Controlo de tráfego indexado a uma classe de rota IPV6 tristate Tem IPv6 — built-in se o endereço é atribuído antes dos módulos São booleanos, portanto «fazer disto um módulo» não é opção e a pergunta passa a ser se os ativar de todo. Um kernel sem IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES continua a encaminhar; apenas ignora todas as tabelas secundárias, e os comandos ip rule parecem funcionar sem fazer nada. 05 Netfilter, conntrack, NAT # núcleo: tudo o resto depende disto CONFIG_NETFILTER=y CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK=m <M> a tabela de estados CONFIG_NF_NAT=m <M> motor NAT, necessário ao MASQUERADE CONFIG_NF_TABLES=m <M> o núcleo do nftables CONFIG_NF_TABLES_INET=m <M> uma tabela para v4 e v6 CONFIG_NFT_CT=m <M> expressão ct CONFIG_NETFILTER_XTABLES=m <M> camada de compatibilidade xtables CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_MASQUERADE=m CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK_FTP=m # helpers: carregar só o necessário Símbolo Forma Efeito se faltar NF_CONNTRACK tristate Sem regras com estado, sem NAT, sem ferramenta conntrack NF_NAT tristate MASQUERADE e DNAT simplesmente não existem NF_TABLES tristate nft responde que não existe ou não é suportado NETFILTER_XTABLES tristate Regras iptables legadas falham ao aplicar NF_CONNTRACK_FTP etc. tristate Só falta o helper desse protocolo — bom padrão Módulos servem — até desativar módulos Debian e todas as distribuições principais trazem o netfilter como módulos, e funciona. Compile dentro quando pretende pôr kernel.modules_disabled=1 depois do arranque, ou quando a firewall tem de poder descartar pacotes antes de qualquer processo de utilizador correr. 06 Bridges, VLANs, bonds, links virtuais Símbolo Recomendado Necessário para BRIDGE <M> Tudo o que faz bridge: VMs, contentores, o switch do GNS3 BRIDGE_NETFILTER <M> iptables em tráfego comutado; o Docker precisa VLAN_8021Q <M> ip link add ... type vlan BONDING <M> Bonds LACP e de failover MACVLAN / IPVLAN <M> Muitos endereços numa NIC, rede de contentores VETH <M> Nam

kingdomOfTUIs: Terminal Handbook · Application Atlas Kingdom of TUIs A terminal user interface is a program that owns the screen of your terminal and behaves like an application: a file manager with panels, a monitor with graphs, a Git client with staging, a database browser. No window manager, no mouse required, no browser engine — just cells, keys and colour. This page is a field guide to the applications you can actually install on Linux today, with their GitHub projects, so you can jump straight to the source and the README. Everything below runs inside a plain terminal on Linux. Most are single binaries or small packages; a few need a helper service (music players that speak MPD, for example). The lists are organised by what you are trying to get done, not by language or framework, because that is how you will look for them. If a project is marked popular , it is one of the ones with the largest GitHub communities — a proxy for documentation, issues answered, and years of bug reports. Rust · Linux, macOS ranger The classic three-column, vi-inspired file manager. Python, previews, bookmarks, and a plugin ecosystem that has aged well. Python · Linux, macOS, BSD lf Ranger's spirit written in Go: one binary, configurable keybindings, shell integration, and no Python runtime to carry around. Go · Linux, macOS, BSD nnn Very small C file manager with a plugin system, session handling and batch operations. The one to install on a rescue system. C · Linux, macOS, BSD Vifm Dual-pane file manager with genuine Vim keybindings, registers and a command line. Feels like editing a filesystem. Rust · Linux, macOS Superfile A modern-looking two-pane manager with themes and a friendly default keymap. Aimed at people who find ranger too spartan. Go · Linux, macOS joshuto Ranger-like columns and previews in Rust, with a configuration file you can actually read in one sitting. Rust · Linux, macOS xplr A hackable file explorer built around piping and Lua configuration. More of a toolkit than a fixed application. Rust · Linux, macOS System monitoring 7 btop++ popular CPU, memory, disks, network and processes with real graphs and themes. The modern replacement for top in most setups.
